questions.question: For non-negative losses, $X\le_eY$ means $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{\alpha X}]\le\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{\alpha Y}]$. Which requirement on the risk-aversion argument $\alpha$ belongs to this order?
options: It holds for at least one $\alpha>0$.
The inequality holds for every $\alpha>0$.
It holds only at $\alpha=0$.
It holds only at the largest observed loss.

questions.question: For non-negative losses, exponential order tests $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{\alpha X}]$ at every $\alpha>0$. An analyst instead compares $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha X}]$ and $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha Y}]$. What has changed?
options: The decreasing test is different from the positive exponential test.
Only notation changed; the two test families are identical.
Only the units of the loss amounts changed.
Only the mean is tested by the negative exponent.

questions.question: Two non-negative loss laws have $M_X(0)=M_Y(0)=1$, where $M$ denotes exponential expectation. Does this equality alone establish exponential order in both directions?
options: Yes; equality at zero identifies the entire law.
Yes; continuity forces equality at every positive argument.
No; a valid MGF must equal zero at the origin.
No; all loss laws share this equality at zero.

questions.question: Non-negative losses satisfy $X\le_eY$ and $Y\le_eZ$, with positive exponential moments allowed to be infinite. What comparison follows for X and Z?
options: $Z\le_eX$.
The inference requires all three means to be equal.
$X\le_eZ$.
The inference requires independent realisations of the losses.

questions.question: Integrable non-negative losses satisfy stop-loss order $X\le_{\mathrm{sl}}Y$, equivalently comparison by all increasing convex tests. Why does this imply exponential order?
options: $x\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{\alpha x}$ is increasing convex for $\alpha>0$.
$x\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{\alpha x}$ is decreasing concave for $\alpha>0$.
Exponential order compares only the common mean.
Every increasing convex test must be an exponential.

questions.question: $X=1$ surely and Y equals 0 or 2 with equal probabilities. At $\alpha=\log2$, where log is natural, what is $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{\alpha Y}]-\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{\alpha X}]$?
Loss X is Bernoulli with probability $0.2$ and loss Y is Bernoulli with probability $0.4$, each taking 0 or 1. For every $\alpha>0$, which difference establishes $X\le_eY$?
options: $M_Y(\alpha)-M_X(\alpha)=0.2\mathrm{e}^\alpha$.
$M_Y(\alpha)-M_X(\alpha)=0.2(\mathrm{e}^\alpha-1)>0$.
$M_Y(\alpha)-M_X(\alpha)=-0.2(\mathrm{e}^\alpha-1)<0$.
$M_Y(\alpha)-M_X(\alpha)=0.2$ for all positive arguments.

questions.question: Loss X is exponential with rate 2 and loss Y exponential with rate 1. Their finite MGFs are $r/(r-\alpha)$ for rate r. At $\alpha=1/2$, which pair $(M_X,M_Y)$ is obtained?

Initial wealth is $w=3$, utility is $u(v)=-\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha v}$ with $\alpha=\log2$, and final wealth is $w-L$. Loss X is 1 surely; Y is 0 or 2 with equal probabilities. Which pair of expected utilities $(\mathbb{E}[u(w-X)],\mathbb{E}[u(w-Y)])$ is correct?
Loss amounts are re-expressed as $X^*=100X$ and $Y^*=100Y$. To reproduce the old exponential test at positive argument $\alpha$ using the new amounts, which new argument is required?
options: $100\alpha$.
$\alpha$.

questions.question: For exponentially ordered losses $X\le_eY$, a variance comparison follows when their means agree and MGFs are finite near zero. Why is finiteness near zero part of that statement?
options: It makes every positive-argument MGF finite automatically.
It replaces the need for equal means.
It supports the moment comparison underlying the local expansion.
It forces the two MGFs to agree identically.

questions.question: Loss X is 0 or 2 with equal probabilities, while Y equals 2 surely. Since $X\le2$ always, $X\le_eY$. What does this example show about a variance comparison without equal means?
options: It must hold: X has variance no larger than Y.
It cannot be assessed because the MGFs are infinite.
It cannot be assessed because their means agree.
It can fail: X has variance 1 and Y has variance 0.

questions.question: For utility $u(v)=-\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha v}$ with $\alpha>0$ and losses X,Y with finite positive exponential moments, $\mathbb{E}[u(w-L)]=-\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha w}M_L(\alpha)$. If $M_X(\alpha)<M_Y(\alpha)$, can changing their common initial wealth w reverse their expected-utility ranking?
options: Yes; sufficiently large wealth reverses the factor sign.
No; the common negative factor preserves the reverse ranking.
Yes; w changes the loss MGF argument to zero.
No; the two expected utilities become exactly equal.

questions.question: Loss X is exponential with rate 2 and Y with rate 1. At positive argument $\alpha=3/2$, the rule gives $M_X(\alpha)=4$ while $M_Y(\alpha)=\infty$. Is $M_X(\alpha)\le M_Y(\alpha)$ valid under the extended-value convention?
options: Yes; a finite value is no larger than positive infinity.
No; every valid comparison must have finite moments.
No; the moment difference must first be a real number.
No; the exponential-rate formula gives Y a negative moment.

questions.question: Loss X equals 2 surely, and Y equals 1 or 3 with equal probabilities. Their equal means are 2 and Jensen gives $X\le_eY$. Which variance pair $(\operatorname{Var}X,\operatorname{Var}Y)$ is consistent with the equal-mean implication?
Independent Bernoulli losses X and Y have positive-loss probabilities $1/4$ and $3/4$. They satisfy $X\le_eY$. What is $\mathbb{P}(X>Y)$ under this supplied independent coupling?

Loss Y is 0 or 3 with probabilities $0.6,0.4$, while X equals 2 surely. Thus Y has smaller mean. At $\alpha=\log3$, their exponential moments are $M_Y=11.4$ and $M_X=9$. Does the smaller mean establish $Y\le_eX$?
options: No; this positive exponential test violates the required inequality.
Yes; comparing means is sufficient for exponential order.
Yes; bounded loss supports rule out any test reversal.
No; a single test can never settle an order claim.

questions.question: Let $\mathbb{P}(X=n)=1/[n(n+1)]$ for integers $n\ge1$, and let $Y=2X$. For every $\alpha>0$, both exponential expectations diverge. Under extended values, does mutual exponential order identify the two loss laws here?
options: Yes; mutual comparison always invokes finite-MGF uniqueness.
No; both directions compare infinities while the laws differ.
Yes; scaling a non-negative law leaves its support unchanged.
No; the probabilities of X fail to sum to one.

questions.question: Loss X equals 1 surely. Loss Y is 0 with probability $1-p$ and 2 with probability $p\in[0,1]$. Put $z=\mathrm{e}^\alpha>1$. Their moment difference is $(z-1)(pz+p-1)$. Which p values give $X\le_eY$ for every positive argument?
options: $p>0$ is enough.
$p=1$ is required.

questions.question: Loss X is 0 or 2 with equal probabilities. Y is 0, 1, 3 with probabilities $1/3,1/2,1/6$. Both have mean 1 and second moment 2. Put $z=\mathrm{e}^\alpha>1$. What exponential comparison holds for every positive $\alpha$?
options: $Y\le_eX$ strictly at every positive argument.
Both directions hold because the first two moments match.
Neither direction holds because the variances match.
$X\le_eY$ strictly at every positive argument.
